Volume 15 · Chapter 04

Development, poverty and structural change

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v15-c03

By the endCompare poverty-reduction mechanisms and their institutional constraints.

Volume 15 · Chapter 4

Capability and prerequisites

Compare a policy's measured poverty effect, its economic mechanism and its credible causal evidence. A fall in a headcount, a new loan and a move out of agriculture are different observations; none alone establishes a lasting welfare improvement.

Prerequisites. Use the market conduct and entry analysis in Chapter 3. Also use labor and education, public budgets, and experimental assignment. All numerical populations below are synthetic. Monetary amounts are units of a stated real consumption good per person or period; no example uses a current international poverty line.

1. Decide what deprivation means before computing it

A ministry can report fewer poor households after a program even while the poorest people become poorer. It might count households rather than people, change its price deflator, lose migrant respondents, or target only families just below a threshold. A defensible evaluation therefore fixes a welfare concept, population, price basis, poverty line and observation period before comparing policies. Here y is nonnegative real consumption per person. Income, wealth and consumption answer different questions: a loan raises cash available today but also creates a liability; selling assets can maintain consumption while reducing resilience. Health, learning, safety and political agency also matter. A monetary index measures one specified dimension and cannot establish all of these capabilities.

Let wᵢ≥0 be population weights with Σwᵢ=1, and let z>0 be a fixed real poverty line. Define gᵢ=max{1−yᵢ/z,0}. The weighted Foster–Greer–Thorbecke family is P₀=Σwᵢ1{yᵢ<z}, and Pα=Σwᵢgᵢ^α for α>0. We use α=1 and 2 for depth and squared-gap severity. The strict inequality convention treats an observation exactly on the line as nonpoor; it avoids the undefined expression 0⁰. The World Bank's poverty handbook, Chapter 4, presents these measures, their subgroup decomposition and their differing sensitivity to deprivation. Our proofs and allocations below are original finite-population applications.

Decomposition. Partition the population into disjoint groups G with shares Wᴳ=Σᵢ∈ᴳwᵢ. For each positive-share group calculate Pαᴳ with weights wᵢ/Wᴳ. Expanding ΣᴳWᴳPαᴳ reproduces each individual term exactly once, so Pα=ΣᴳWᴳPαᴳ. Zero-share groups contribute zero and need no conditional index. Changing composition changes the aggregate even with unchanged within-group poverty. With two dates the exact identity is ΔP=ΣᴳWᴳ₀ΔPᴳ+ΣᴳΔWᴳPᴳ₁. It is an accounting identity, not a causal attribution of migration or policy.

Transfers and the objective. For y<z, a small consumption increase reduces P₁ at rate w/z and P₂ at rate 2w(z−y)/z². For equal-weight people, move t>0 from a richer poor person y₂ to a poorer person y₁, keeping their order and both below z. P₁ stays constant. Their contribution to P₂ changes by 2wt(t−(y₂−y₁))/z², which is strictly negative for 0<t≤(y₂−y₁)/2. Headcount is unchanged. Thus these indexes embody distinct priorities; the data cannot choose the ethical weight on depth for us.

For an outside-funded transfer budget B, fixed prices and no behavioral response, eliminating all measured gaps costs N z P₁ in an equal-weight population of N. This is a lower engineering cost conditional on perfect information and costless delivery, not a fiscal forecast. If delivery consumes resources, recipients save part of the transfer, suppliers raise prices, or taxpayers are themselves near poverty, the consumption accounting must be redone. Transfers within the measured population must subtract the donor's loss. Survey expansion weights should represent persons, with household size handled consistently; weighting does not by itself recover unequal allocation within a household.

Worked case 1. The least expensive exit versus the deepest gap

Four equally weighted people consume (2,6,9,15), with 10. The gaps are (8/10,4/10,1/10,0), giving (P0,P1,P2)=(3/4,13/40,81/400). A one-unit progressive transfer from the second to the first produces (3,5,9,15), hence (P0,P1,P2)=(3/4,13/40,3/16). The headcount misses the improvement under a severity-sensitive criterion.

Now an external sponsor has 4 units and pays this real resource cost. To minimize headcount, at least one person can exit by filling the one-unit gap of the person at nine. Two exits cost at least 1+4=5, so no feasible allocation achieves more than one. One optimal allocation gives that person one and the person at six three, yielding (2,9,10,15) and (1/2,9/40,13/80). In contrast, minimizing P₂ gives all four units to the poorest person: (6,6,9,15) yields (3/4,9/40,33/400). Both spend four and reduce the total gap by four, yet their headcounts disagree.

For the severity optimum, no money should go above z while a positive gap remains. On the relevant compact feasible set the squared-gap objective is convex. Its derivative in a recipient's transfer is most negative at the lowest consumption. Moving an infinitesimal amount from a better-off recipient to a poorer recipient therefore reduces the objective until their levels equalize or a transfer reaches zero. This exchange argument, or the supporting-gradient inequality for a convex function, proves the resulting equalization allocation globally optimal. Here four units only bring the poorest up to six. Headcount minimization instead orders the costs of complete exits; it has no reward for a partial gap reduction.

Missing observations are a separate uncertainty. If response share 0<r≤1 is known and observed gap scores gᵢ^α have mean p among respondents, nonnegative consumption implies Pα∈[rp,rp+1−r] for α>0. The same lower and upper bounds hold for headcount when p is the respondent poverty share. Set every missing person's consumption at or above z for the lower endpoint and at zero for the upper endpoint, proving both endpoints sharp. Population mixtures with freely divisible missing mass attain every intermediate headcount; for a fixed finite set of people with fixed weights, feasible headcounts can instead be discrete. For α>0, continuously varying missing consumption between zero and z attains the intermediate gap-index values. These bounds are about missing outcomes, not sampling error. Without restrictions on missingness, reweighting observed respondents need not collapse them. A threshold comparison should also report sensitivity to plausible real-price and equivalence-scale choices.

2. Credit can change feasibility without creating productivity

Consider an entrepreneur with liquid wealth w≥0 at date zero. At date one an inactive entrepreneur has Rw, where R>0 is both the gross saving return and the lender's opportunity cost. An active project uses a fixed setup resource F>0 and working capital k≥0 today and produces A√k real goods tomorrow, A>0; no setup input is recovered. Borrowing b≤b̄ is contractually enforceable and repaid at Rb. There is no default, hidden action or lender operating cost in this deliberately narrow model. These exclusions allow us to isolate a cash constraint without pretending to explain every credit market.

If F+k≤w+b̄, using own funds first and borrowing the shortfall gives terminal wealth Rw+π(k), where π(k)=A√k−R(F+k). If there are unused own funds they earn R; if borrowing is needed its repayment subtracts exactly the same opportunity cost. Thus comparing profits with zero already compares the project with saving all wealth. The feasible maximum working capital is K=w+b̄−F. If K<0, entry is infeasible. Otherwise the best active capital is k̂=min{K,(A/(2R))²}: on k>0 the derivative A/(2√k)−R changes sign only once, and strict concavity ensures a global maximum. At K=0, profit is −RF, so inactivity wins. Enter only if π(k̂)>0; at equality both choices are optimal, and our reporting convention selects inactivity.

The unconstrained maximum profit is A²/(4R)−RF. When A²<4R²F, no wealth or credit expansion can make the project worthwhile. At equality the unconstrained active allocation only ties inactivity. When A²>4R²F, write t=√k. Positive surplus requires Rt²−At+RF<0, hence k lies strictly between the squares of t₋=(A−√(A²−4R²F))/(2R) and t₊ with the plus sign. A constrained entrepreneur chooses entry precisely when K>t₋². Consequently an increase in the loan ceiling may do nothing for an entrepreneur too far below setup feasibility, then trigger a discrete entry decision, and later raise capital smoothly until the unconstrained optimum. This is a one-period activation threshold, not a proved dynamic poverty trap.

Worked case 2. Identical productivity, different feasible projects

Set (A,F,R,loan ceiling)=(8,4,1,3). The unconstrained capital and profit are (16,12). At wealth (0,2,5), the chosen capital and incremental profit are respectively ((0,0),(1,3),(4,8)), where capital zero in the first pair denotes inactivity, not payment of the setup cost. At wealth two the household supplies two, borrows three and purchases five units of inputs; production is eight, repayment three and terminal consumption five. The lender advances three and receives three, exactly its opportunity cost. Consolidated incremental resources are output eight minus inputs five, or three. Borrowing is not an additional benefit in that sum.

At wealth five, inputs cost eight, the loan is three and output is sixteen. Terminal wealth is thirteen, versus five under inactivity. The credit limit changes the choice; it does not identify why the limit exists. A grant or guarantee requires a payer account, and an uncertain-output extension requires a default rule and expected lender losses. Even here, increasing the ceiling by one may change entry for one wealth level and only scale for another. An observed average take-up effect therefore does not identify a universal marginal return to capital.

The Hyderabad microcredit experiment studied access through neighborhood assignment. Its authors discuss selection into borrowing, cross-area access and reasons to emphasize intention-to-treat effects. Read the bounded design discussion in Banerjee, Duflo, Glennerster and Kinnan, March 2014 working version, introduction and Section 3. Our deterministic project is not their estimated model, and we infer no numerical effect from that experiment for the synthetic entrepreneur. The useful lesson is to distinguish the financial contract, assignment to access, actual borrowing and household outcomes.

3. Health and education can be complements

A low observed education return may reflect a missing complement rather than low learning technology. Conversely, a positive schooling association may reflect selection. To make the mechanism precise, let a person choose schooling e∈{0,1} and a health-enabling investment h∈{0,1}. These are economic labels for two costly inputs, not clinical recommendations. Incremental real output is a e+b h+c eh, with a,b,c≥0; it accrues to this person as income and entails no omitted employer loss. Schooling costs Cₑ>0 and health investment Cₕ>0 in real resources at date zero, with gross discount factor one. Output arrives later. The person is risk neutral, cannot borrow and must meet Cₑe+Cₕh≤w. An outside endowment supplies consumption needed for survival and is unchanged across options, so spending investible wealth does not violate a subsistence constraint.

There are exactly four bundles. Their net gains are 0, a−Cₑ, b−Cₕ and a+b+c−Cₑ−Cₕ; delete infeasible bundles and take the largest, retaining ties. This enumeration is a complete global solution, including liquidity corners. The incremental benefit of schooling rises from a to a+c when h becomes available. The cross difference is c, a technological complementarity; it is neither a regression coefficient nor proof that any actual treatment and school program interact this way. A health spillover ηh benefiting neighbors can be added to social surplus but not to the person's private objective. A planner without the private liquidity limit compares the same four values plus ηh, provided its own budget can purchase the chosen inputs.

Worked case 3. A profitable bundle that nobody can finance alone

Let (a,b,c,Ce,Ch,w,neighbor benefit)=(1,1,4,2,2,2,1). Private net gains over all bundles (none, schooling, health, both) are (0,-1,-1,2). Both investments would cost four, exceeding wealth two, so the private optimum is neither. Their social gains including the specified neighbor benefit are (0,-1,0,3). This does not make a free policy available: someone must supply the missing resources.

An outside treasury with an existing endowment pays two units to provide h directly. Once h is supplied, schooling's extra output is five at cost two; the person voluntarily spends their two on e. Relative to no intervention, their output rises by six and their own resource expense by two, a private net gain of four. The neighbor gains one and the treasury loses two, giving (private,neighbor,treasury,total)=(4,1,-2,3). Health provision without the induced schooling would produce private gain one, neighbor gain one and treasury cost two, total zero. The complement is the reason the funded package improves total surplus here.

A cash grant of one leaves total investible wealth three; both remain infeasible and each single input remains privately unprofitable. The person keeps the grant, a transfer matched by the treasury's loss, with no new production. A grant of two makes the joint bundle affordable and yields the same real investment surplus as direct provision if it induces that choice. Administrative cost, crowd-out, unequal access and alternative uses of public funds can reverse a policy ranking. None is silently assumed away in an empirical claim: they are explicit omissions from this model to be measured in an application.

A factorial experiment can randomize offers of the two inputs and compare the four assignment means. Under full compliance and no interference, the difference-in-differences of those means identifies an average interaction in potential outcomes. With selective take-up it identifies an interaction between offers, not necessarily c. If the health offer changes attendance even without recorded treatment, an instrumental-variable exclusion restriction needs a new argument. Track actual learning and functioning separately from enrollment, attendance, spending and provider receipts. A transfer to a provider is a fiscal expense; resources used by the provider are the social cost. Counting both as separate resource losses would double count.

4. Structural transformation requires demand and prices

Structural transformation means activity shifting across broad sectors; the Herrendorf–Rogerson–Valentinyi review abstract frames this reallocation and motivates multisector analysis. The following complete two-sector economy is our own stripped-down illustration. It does not claim to reproduce the review's full model or any country's path.

A representative household supplies one unit of labor inelastically. Competitive firms produce food a=A Lₐ and manufactures m=B Lₘ, with A,B>0, Lₐ+Lₘ=1 and no fixed costs. The household owns firms, which earn zero profit at equilibrium. Manufactures are the numeraire; food price is p. Utility is (a−ā)^θ m^(1−θ) for a>ā and m>0, with ā>0 and 0<θ<1. Assume A>ā so that a strictly feasible consumption bundle exists. A household desiring both goods and free mobility force a common wage W=pA=B, hence p=B/A. If one sector paid strictly less, no labor would enter it; if it paid strictly more, labor would leave the other, contradicting positive demand for both.

After purchasing subsistence food, discretionary income is B−pā>0. Maximizing the log of utility gives expenditure shares θ and 1−θ on discretionary food and manufactures. Strict concavity of the log on its domain proves the first-order allocation globally unique; utility approaches zero at either relevant boundary, excluding a boundary optimum. Therefore a=ā+θ(B−pā)/p and m=(1−θ)(B−pā). Market clearing gives Lₐ=θ+(1−θ)ā/A and Lₘ=(1−θ)(1−ā/A). Both shares are strictly between zero and one, so the proposed wages indeed support positive sectoral production and exhaust the labor endowment. This constructs and establishes uniqueness of the interior equilibrium.

Higher A reduces the agricultural labor share: dLₐ/dA=−(1−θ)ā/A². Agriculture becomes more productive while employing fewer workers because subsistence needs absorb a shrinking portion of resources. If ā=0, the share is θ regardless of A; productivity growth alone no longer shifts labor under these homothetic preferences. Higher B raises the common wage in manufactured units but leaves the labor shares unchanged in this special model. With A≤ā there is no bundle with both a>ā and m>0: the maintained utility domain is infeasible, not an interior equilibrium with a negative manufacturing share. Trade, land ownership, migration costs and services would change this economy and must be modeled before drawing country-specific conclusions.

Worked case 4. A productive farm sector releases labor

Take (theta,subsistence,A0,A1,B)=(1/3,1,4,8,2). Initially (food price,agricultural labor,food,manufactures)=(1/2,1/2,2,1). After A doubles, (1/4,5/12,10/3,7/6). The common wage remains two manufactured units, but food becomes cheaper and the household can attain higher utility. Current-price output equals the wage at both dates; that nominal equality is not zero growth in real consumption.

For a transparent quantity account fix food's valuation at the initial price one half. Sector output per worker at those prices changes from (2,2) to (4,2). Aggregate output at fixed prices rises from two to 17/6. With Y=ΣLⱼqⱼ, subtracting the two dates gives ΔY=ΣLⱼ₀Δqⱼ+ΣΔLⱼqⱼ₁. Here (within,reallocation,total)=(1,-1/6,5/6). Reallocation is negative under this exact convention because labor exits the sector with higher final measured output per worker. It does not mean mobility reduced welfare: the relative-price change and subsistence demand made this equilibrium optimal for the household. Evaluating reallocation at initial productivity instead would move the interaction term into the within component. State the convention before interpreting a decomposition.

The same accounting warns against comparing rural and urban average earnings as if their gap were a migration treatment effect. Worker sorting, hours, amenities, land income, skills and local prices can differ. A move can raise a worker's real consumption even with unchanged nominal earnings, or reduce it despite higher earnings. Aggregate productivity is not a sufficient statistic for poverty: trace ownership, wages, prices and fiscal incidence back to the distribution of real consumption used in Section 1.

5. Design evidence around the policy mechanism

Let village saturation s denote the fraction offered a program and let D be actual participation. An assignment effect compares potential outcomes under two specified offer rules; a receipt effect compares treatment status under a defined surrounding exposure. They coincide only with additional compliance and interference assumptions. Under no interference, random encouragement Z, exclusion, monotone take-up and a nonzero first stage yield the familiar complier ratio: E[Y|Z=1]−E[Y|Z=0]=Pr(complier)E[Y(1)−Y(0)|complier], while the take-up difference equals Pr(complier). The always and never takers cancel. If Z changes neighbors' participation or local prices, their outcomes need not cancel, and division by the first stage does not repair exclusion.

For a two-stage saturation design, randomize many independent villages to s=0 or s=1/2, then randomly choose half the people in the latter villages. Assume full compliance for the worked case and partial interference: outcomes depend on one's own d and the village's total fraction g, but not on identities or other villages. Define Yᵢ(d,g), including the individual's own treatment in g. Within half-treated villages g is held fixed when comparing selected and unselected people; under random selection their difference in expectation identifies the population-average direct contrast at g=1/2. Comparing unselected people there with people in untreated villages identifies an indirect contrast. No treated person exists at g=0, so the design cannot identify a direct effect at zero exposure without another supported assignment rule.

The proof uses known assignment probabilities. For any supported exposure (d,g) with probability πᵢ(d,g)>0, E[1{exposure=(d,g)}Yᵢ/πᵢ(d,g)]=Yᵢ(d,g). Average across the prespecified target individuals and subtract exposures. This Horvitz–Thompson identity requires consistency for the exposure mapping; if neighbor identities matter beyond g, the stated potential outcome is misspecified. Villages, not their individual records, are independent units for uncertainty when interference is contained within villages. A small number of villages requires inference justified for that actual randomization; merely clustering a regression does not manufacture many independent observations.

Worked case 5. A spillover makes the naive Wald ratio too large

Every village has 4 people. In a synthetic full-compliance population let (baseline,direct coefficient,spillover coefficient,saturation)=(4,2,1,1/2), so Y(d,g)=4+2d+g. Exactly two people are selected in a half-treated village. Their outcome is 13/2, the two unselected people's outcome is 9/2, and everyone in a zero village has four. Therefore (direct,indirect,policy mean effect)=(2,1/2,3/2). The policy mean moves from four to 11/2; take-up moves from zero to one half. Dividing yields 3, not the direct coefficient two. The extra one reflects spillovers relative to the treatment first stage.

Suppose instead only 4/5 of people respond in treated-policy villages, their observed mean is 11/2, and every outcome lies in the closed support [0,10]. Control mean four is fully observed. Without a missingness restriction the policy effect lies in the closed interval [2/5,12/5]. Assign all missing outcomes zero or ten to attain the endpoints; randomization of offers did not randomize survey response. This is a different incomplete-data scenario from the fully observed structural illustration, not a claim that its deterministic outcomes suddenly become unknown.

A prospective protocol records village eligibility, allocation probabilities, take-up, exposure, real consumption, outcomes of nonrecipients, delivery costs and missingness by arm. It fixes a price basis and follow-up horizon, and protects assignment concealment before enrollment. A target region may have different credit enforcement, illness burden, school capacity or product demand. Conditional response stability, overlap and a correct target covariate distribution are additional transport assumptions. A pilot estimate should be paired with a test of the mechanism most likely to change at scale—for example, provider capacity or local wage response—and a funded stopping or revision rule.

6. Exercises

State assumptions before applying a formula. Exact fractions or equivalent decimals are acceptable. Questions 1–9 have determinate components; Question 10 is assessed by the explicit criteria in its solution.

  1. For Case 1 partition the first two people into group R and the last two into group U. Compute each group's three poverty measures and recover the national measures. Explain why equal household weights can fail for a person-level target.
  2. With Case 1's four-unit external budget, prove that (6,6,9,15) globally minimizes squared-gap poverty, yet cannot minimize headcount. What is the minimum budget eliminating all poverty in this fixed-consumption accounting?
  3. In Case 2 replace the loan ceiling by zero, keeping wealth five. Solve entry, capital, output and terminal wealth. Then derive the strict wealth threshold for entry when the original ceiling three is restored, including the equality case.
  4. An entrepreneur has A=3,F=4,R=1 and arbitrarily large wealth. Prove that no credit ceiling expansion produces voluntary entry. Explain why this refutes the claim that every nonborrower needs a bigger loan.
  5. For Case 3 compare a one-unit unrestricted grant, a two-unit unrestricted grant and direct health provision costing two. Give private, treasury and neighbor changes, real total surplus, and the induced bundles. State which accounting items cancel.
  6. In the health/education model a factorial randomized assignment has full compliance and no interference. Derive the interaction contrast in output and in net output. Then explain exactly what changes if assignment induces selective take-up.
  7. Derive Case 4's equilibrium again with ā=0. Give both agricultural labor shares and fixed-initial-price output growth. Why does the original subsistence term matter for transformation?
  8. Use the original Case 4 to decompose output growth with final labor shares and initial sector productivity instead. Reconcile this with the earlier decomposition by calculating the interaction term.
  9. In Case 5 prove the exposure inverse-probability identity, compute the naive Wald ratio, and derive the stated attrition bounds. Give a target population response law with the same baseline and direct coefficient but a different policy mean effect; identify the untested transport assumption.
  10. A ministry proposes scaling a loan-plus-school program because participant income rose and the poverty headcount fell. Write a compact decision protocol covering measurement, financing, causal design, health complementarity, spillovers, attrition and scale. Specify evidence that would lead you to revise the recommendation.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Subgroup accounting

R has gaps 4/5 and 2/5, so its (P₀,P₁,P₂) is (1,3/5,2/5). U has gaps 1/10 and zero, hence (1/2,1/20,1/200). Each group has half the people; the weighted average is (3/4,13/40,81/400). The normalization is within each group before multiplying by its population share, not an unweighted average when shares differ. If a poor household has six members and a nonpoor household has one, equal household weights report half poor while person weights report six sevenths under equal within-household consumption. The latter assumption itself requires scrutiny; neither scheme identifies unobserved distribution within the family.

2. A global allocation comparison

Let transfers tᵢ≥0 sum to at most four and fᵢ(t)=max(10−yᵢ−t,0)²/400. At t*=(4,0,0,0), the gradient is (−8/400,−8/400,−2/400,0). Convexity gives f(t)−f(t*)≥∇f(t*)·(t−t*). Because total spending is at most four, the right side is nonnegative: moving expenditure away from the first coordinate to the second ties its marginal value, and moving it to the third or fourth loses value. This establishes global optimality, not just a local first-order condition. The resulting P₂ is 33/400. Headcount remains 3/4, whereas allocating one unit to the person at nine attains 1/2; two exits require five, so 1/2 is optimal. Filling all three gaps costs 13. That is a consumption-gap accounting cost with an external payer and costless delivery, not a forecast including tax distortions or price responses.

3. Lending changes a feasible set

Without borrowing, wealth five leaves K=1 after setup. Since the unconstrained k is sixteen, choose k=1; profit 8−5=3>0. Output eight is consumed at date one and terminal wealth is eight, versus five without entry. Thus (k,output,terminal wealth,incremental surplus)=(1,8,8,3). With ceiling three, K=w−1. The lower root is t₋=4−√12 and entry requires w−1>(4−√12)². Hence w>29−16√3, approximately 1.28718708. At equality the best active allocation gives zero surplus and ties inactivity; our convention chooses inactivity. Below w=1 even setup is infeasible, while intermediate wealth can finance some capital yet still not cover the fixed cost in present value. The strict threshold follows from the lower profit root and the location of the concave maximum, not from merely having a positive loan balance.

4. A missing productive opportunity

Writing t=√k, profit is 3t−t²−4=−(t−3/2)²−7/4. Its maximum is -7/4, strictly below zero even with unlimited capital. Every feasible capital set is a subset of the unconstrained set, so no ceiling increase changes that conclusion. Inactivity maximizes terminal wealth. A nonborrower may lack a worthwhile project rather than cash, may value flexibility, or may face risk omitted from this example. The model proves the first possibility; it does not identify which explanation applies in actual data. Subsidizing this project without valuing some omitted benefit would create a resource loss, even if loan disbursement and recorded business activity increased.

5. Separate transfers from inputs

A grant of one increases investible wealth to three. The only feasible active bundles are the individually unprofitable ones, so the person chooses neither and retains the grant. Changes (private,neighbor,treasury,total) are (1,0,-1,0). A grant of two makes the four-unit joint investment feasible; its own net production gain is two, and the person also receives the grant. Changes are (4,1,-2,3). Direct health provision costing two induces schooling and gives the same four, one, minus two, three accounting: the person receives output six and spends two. Both successful policies consume four real units and produce six plus one external benefit. The grant itself cancels against the payer loss; the input expense does not. The equivalence depends on known choices, the given costs and no delivery losses. Liquidity relief does not establish that unrestricted cash and in-kind provision are generally interchangeable.

6. Which interaction is identified?

Under full compliance the four mean incremental outputs are 0,a,b,a+b+c, so μ₁₁−μ₁₀−μ₀₁+μ₀₀=c. Subtracting the additive resource costs Cₑe+Cₕh leaves exactly the same interaction because each cost appears once with each sign. In Case 3 the contrast is 4. Random assignment identifies these assignment means without assuming a production function, provided there is no attrition or interference and all arms have positive assignment probability. With noncompliance, potential outcomes are indexed by offers and their induced bundles; the mean contrast remains an offer interaction. Selection into receipt can differ across all four cells. Recovering c then needs credible restrictions linking offers, actual inputs and outcomes, rather than simply relabeling the reduced-form contrast. If health provision changes peers' learning, the no-interference premise also fails.

7. Homothetic demand removes this reallocation channel

With ā=0, discretionary income is the whole wage B. Food expenditure is θB, p=B/A, so a=θA and Lₐ=θ. Manufacturing is (1−θ)B. Both dates therefore have labor shares (1/3,1/3). At initial food price one half, initial output is (1/2)(4/3)+4/3=2, while final output is (1/2)(8/3)+4/3=8/3, giving 2/3. Every worker's allocation remains in the same sectoral proportions: the household spends a fixed share on food. Positive subsistence in the original model caused the food budget share to decline as agricultural productivity made the subsistence bundle cheaper. Other preference or technology mechanisms can also create structural transformation; this calculation isolates one.

8. The interaction is reassigned

Use ΔY=ΣLⱼ₁Δqⱼ+ΣΔLⱼqⱼ₀. The first term is (5/12)2=5/6. The second is (−1/12)2+(1/12)2=0. The interaction ΣΔLⱼΔqⱼ is (−1/12)2=−1/6, so (within at final shares,reallocation at initial productivity,interaction)=(5/6,0,-1/6). Starting from the earlier within component one, adding the interaction gives five sixths; starting from reallocation at final productivity minus one sixth, subtracting that interaction gives zero. Both conventions sum to the same five-sixths growth. Neither convention identifies the output that would have occurred had a planner forcibly held labor shares fixed while prices, demand and technology adjusted.

9. A design identifies specified exposures

Consistency makes observed Y equal the fixed Yᵢ(d,g) on the event that exposure occurs. Taking expectation of its indicator divided by the known positive probability gives one; multiplying by the fixed potential outcome proves the inverse-probability identity. Averaging and differencing therefore recovers the stated exposure contrast, with cluster dependence retained for uncertainty. In the synthetic law, village mean rises by 3/2 and participation by 1/2, so their ratio is three. Direct receipt at fixed g changes outcomes by two, and untreated exposure changes them by one half. With respondent mean 11/2 and response 4/5, treated mean is between 22/5 and 32/5; subtracting control four yields [2/5,12/5]. No response-independence claim is needed for these sharp endpoints. A target law Y=4+2d+0g preserves baseline and own-treatment coefficient but has half-saturation mean effect 1. Transporting the original total policy effect had additionally assumed a stable spillover response, which the original assignment cannot verify in the new region.

10. A decision protocol that can reject its own premise

First fix person-weighted real consumption, price deflators, a dated local line and the eligible population; show headcount, depth and severity together, plus health and learning outcomes. Audit whether a participant's income rise is real new output, a transfer, asset sale or borrowing. Second specify loan terms, repayment/default, provider resource costs, administrative cost, taxpayer incidence and reserves; reconcile household, lender and treasury accounts. Third randomize a feasible offer rule before enrollment, with a valid comparison group and enough independent clusters; predeclare assignment estimands, supported exposure contrasts and compliant uptake measures without assuming exclusion. A factorial health component can test whether the education offer needs its complement, but its contrast remains an offer effect with noncompliance.

Measure nonrecipient outcomes, provider capacity, prices and attrition. Report support-based missing-outcome bounds as well as an appropriately justified sampling interval. Assess which population and institutional features must remain stable at scale, then run a staged expansion that tests a held-out capacity or spillover prediction. A defensible revision rule suspends expansion if the funded net-resource criterion fails its prespecified threshold, if losses exceed the reserve, or if learning fails to improve despite higher enrollment. An alternative recommendation may favor a smaller or differently targeted program if supported by these accounts. Award equal credit for seven substantive elements: measurement, complete finance, assignment/receipt distinction, health complementarity, interference, missingness/transport and an operational revision rule. Participant before/after growth alone meets none of the causal-design requirement.

7. Teach-back and delayed transfer

Teach-back. In five minutes explain why a four-unit transfer can minimize poverty severity while leaving headcount unchanged; why a loan is not a resource gain; and why an assignment-based Wald ratio can combine direct and spillover effects. A successful explanation states the objective, payer and exposure assumptions before the numerical conclusion.

Delayed retention. After one week, without looking back, derive the credit entry threshold, solve the two-sector labor shares and construct an attrition bound. Then change one primitive in each: raise setup cost until no project is worthwhile, set subsistence to zero, and reduce response so that a policy-effect interval crosses zero. Check the changed results using the original budget, utility domain and outcome support. The criterion is a correct new derivation with boundary cases, not memorization of these examples.

Retention answer guide

Credit: if A²>4R²F, strict entry requires w+b̄−F>[(A−√(A²−4R²F))/(2R)]²; equality ties inactivity. If A²<4R²F every project loses money. Transformation: Lₐ=θ+(1−θ)ā/A, reducing to θ when ā=0. Missing outcomes in [L,U] give an arm mean in [rμ+(1−r)L,rμ+(1−r)U]; subtract the fully observed comparison mean. With Case 5 response changed to one half, its effect interval is [−5/4,15/4], so zero is included. Recheck support and funding rather than transporting the old conclusion.

Next connection. The planned trade and global production chapter will examine what changes when sectoral goods and firms cross borders. Poverty and development evaluation still require tracing those changes to real household resources rather than equating an aggregate output statistic with every person's welfare.

Sources and further study

  • Handbook on Poverty and Inequality, Chapter 4: Measures of Poverty — FGT definitions, headcount/depth/severity distinctions and population-share decomposition; original finite proofs and allocations in manuscript.
  • The miracle of microfinance? Evidence from a randomized evaluation, March 2014 working version — Distinguish access assignment, borrowing selection, neighborhood exposure and intention-to-treat scope; no transported empirical effect claimed.
  • Growth and Structural Transformation, NBER Working Paper18996 — Definition and motivation of sectoral reallocation/multisector analysis only. Original two-sector equilibrium is separately derived.
